flaw_note: trusts Json.NET with TypeNameHandling.All on request bodies
chosen: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-502: with TypeNameHandling.All the $type property in the request chooses which .NET type Json.NET instantiates, and known gadget types turn that into code execution before your JobRequest is ever used. Use TypeNameHandling.None with an explicit discriminator, or a SerializationBinder that allow-lists your job types.
rejected: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. The generic argument JobRequest constrains what Json.NET produces, so $type values pointing at unrelated classes are rejected. TypeNameHandling.All is the documented way to round-trip polymorphic types.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: treats Marshal.load of a client-supplied value as safe because it is base64
prompt:
Rails controller restores a wizard state from a hidden field:

state = Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(params[:state]))

Only our own form ever sets this field.
chosen:
- Verdict: Insecure
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-502: hidden fields are fully client-controlled, and Marshal.load can instantiate arbitrary Ruby objects; known gadget chains in common gems lead to remote code execution.
- Fix: store the state server-side, or serialise to JSON and sign it (ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier).
rejected:
- Verdict: Secure
- vulnerability_count: 0
- The field is only generated by our own form, and Base64 decoding guarantees the payload is well-formed before Marshal sees it.
- Rails escapes params, so injected objects cannot reach the controller.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: misses that global default typing lets the JSON choose classes
chosen: {"verdict": "Insecure", "vulnerability_count": 1, "issues": ["CWE-502"], "summary": "Default typing with a laissez-faire validator lets class names in the JSON pick which types Jackson builds, the setup behind many Jackson gadget-chain RCEs. Remove default typing, or use a strict PolymorphicTypeValidator that allow-lists your own types."}

flaw_note: flags plain Jackson binding to a concrete DTO as insecure deserialisation
chosen: {"verdict": "Secure", "vulnerability_count": 0, "issues": [], "summary": "Without default typing or @JsonTypeInfo, Jackson only instantiates the declared OrderDto and its simple field types; the JSON cannot name classes, so the gadget-chain pattern (CWE-502) does not apply. @Valid adds input validation on top."}

flaw_note: believes node-serialize only restores plain data
chosen:
VERDICT=Insecure COUNT=1
CWE-502: node-serialize revives functions marked with _$$ND_FUNC$$_, and a payload ending in () runs immediately during unserialize, so a crafted cookie executes code on the server. use JSON.parse and validate the fields.
rejected:
VERDICT=Secure COUNT=0
node-serialize produces plain objects like JSON.parse but also keeps Dates and nested types, so reading prefs from the cookie is fine as long as the fields are validated afterwards.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags XXE for Go encoding/xml, which does not process DTD entities
prompt:
Go service unmarshals partner XML:

var inv Invoice
if err := xml.NewDecoder(io.LimitReader(r.Body, 1<<20)).Decode(&inv); err != nil { ... }

Are we exposed to XXE?
chosen: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. Go's encoding/xml does not process DTDs: it never loads external entities or expands custom entity declarations, so the XXE and billion-laughs patterns do not apply here (no CWE-611). The 1 MiB LimitReader already bounds input size, which is the remaining resource concern. Keep using a typed struct as you do.
rejected: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-611: the decoder parses untrusted partner XML without disabling external entities, so a DOCTYPE with a SYSTEM entity can read files from the server.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags XXE although the SAX parser disallows DOCTYPE declarations
chosen:
- Verdict: Secure
- vulnerability_count: 0
- disallow-doctype-decl makes the parser reject any document with a DOCTYPE, so neither external nor recursive entities can be declared (no CWE-611).
- This is the OWASP-recommended setting for Xerces-based SAX parsers; add an upload size cap.
rejected:
- Verdict: Needs changes
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-611: SAXParserFactory resolves external entities by default.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags XXE on .NET 6 XmlDocument, whose resolver is null by default
chosen: {"verdict": "Secure", "vulnerability_count": 0, "issues": [], "summary": "On .NET Core and .NET 5+, XmlDocument's XmlResolver is null by default, so external entities are not resolved (no CWE-611). Don't assign an XmlUrlResolver, and cap the body size."}
rejected: {"verdict": "Insecure", "vulnerability_count": 1, "issues": ["CWE-611"], "summary": "XmlDocument.LoadXml on a request body is a classic XXE sink; set DtdProcessing.Prohibit."}

flaw_note: trusts lxml after the code explicitly re-enables network and entity resolution
prompt:
python import job:

parser = etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=True, no_network=False, load_dtd=True)
tree = etree.fromstring(customer_xml, parser)

we use lxml, which is safe by default, right?
chosen:
VERDICT=Insecure COUNT=1
CWE-611: whatever lxml's defaults are, this parser explicitly loads DTDs, resolves entities and allows network access, so a customer document can pull local files or internal URLs into the parsed tree. use XMLParser(resolve_entities=False, no_network=True, load_dtd=False).
rejected:
VERDICT=Secure COUNT=0
lxml blocks external entities out of the box, so the import job is fine; the extra options only affect DTD validation.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: misses that text/template does no HTML escaping
prompt:
Go handler renders a profile page: import "text/template" var page = template.Must(template.New("p").Parse(`

{{.DisplayName}}

`)) page.Execute(w, user) DisplayName is user-editable. XSS?
chosen: Verdict: Insecure. vulnerability_count: 1. CWE-79: text/template performs no HTML escaping at all, so a display name like <script>…</script> is written into the page as markup. Switch the import to html/template, which escapes contextually; the template text can stay the same.
rejected: Verdict: Secure. vulnerability_count: 0. Go templates escape interpolated values, so {{.DisplayName}} is rendered as text. The template is parsed once at startup with template.Must, which is the recommended pattern.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: misses that triple braces disable Handlebars escaping
prompt:
Handlebars email preview rendered in our admin UI:
{{{message.body}}}
message.body comes from customers. Review.
chosen:
- Verdict: Insecure
- vulnerability_count: 1
- CWE-79: triple braces {{{ }}} output raw, unescaped HTML, so customer markup runs in the admin's session.
- Use {{message.body}}, or sanitise with an allow-list before rendering.
rejected:
- Verdict: Secure
- vulnerability_count: 0
- Handlebars escapes every interpolation by default, so customer content is rendered as text.
- The admin UI is internal, which further limits exposure.
author: claude-draft

flaw_note: flags escaped Handlebars output as XSS
prompt:
handlebars template:

{{ticket.note}}

-- note is free text from users. xss?
chosen:
VERDICT=Secure COUNT=0
double-brace expressions are HTML-escaped by Handlebars, so markup in ticket.note renders as text (no CWE-79). only triple braces or SafeString skip escaping; keep it this way and don't place the value in a script or href.
rejected:
VERDICT=Insecure COUNT=1
CWE-79: ticket.note is user free text rendered into the page.
